what_its_for: Morphine is a strong prescription pain medicine (opioid) used to treat moderate to severe pain that is not well controlled by other pain medicines. It may be used for pain from surgery, cancer, injuries, or other serious medical conditions. Extended-release forms are used for ongoing, around-the-clock pain management.
how_to_take: Take morphine exactly as your doctor prescribes. Swallow tablets or capsules whole with a full glass of water — do not crush, chew, break, or dissolve them, as this can release too much medicine at once and be life-threatening. Some capsules can be opened and sprinkled on soft food like applesauce — ask your pharmacist if this is okay for your specific product. Take with or without food, but if morphine upsets your stomach, taking it with food may help. Never take more than prescribed or take it more often than directed.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on the lowest dose that controls your pain and adjust it based on how you respond. Doses vary widely from person to person depending on your pain level, your body, and your medical history. Do not change your dose on your own. Immediate-release morphine is usually taken every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Extended-release morphine is taken every 8 to 24 hours depending on the specific product. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose of extended-release morphine, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one. For immediate-release morphine taken as needed for pain, take it when you need it for pain relief. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store morphine at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in a secure, locked location away from children and teenagers — accidental ingestion by a child can be fatal. Keep away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep track of how many tablets or capsules you have. Dispose of unused morphine properly — use an authorized drug take-back program or a medicine disposal kiosk near you. If no take-back option is available, you can flush morphine down the toilet according to FDA guidance.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking morphine — this combination can cause dangerous slowing of your breathing and can be fatal. Avoid taking other medicines that cause drowsiness or slow breathing, such as sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines (like Xanax or Valium), muscle relaxers, antihistamines, or other opioids, unless your doctor specifically approves them. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires full alertness until you know how morphine affects you. Avoid stopping morphine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help RIGHT AWAY if you experience: slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; extreme drowsiness or you cannot be woken up; blue or purple color on lips or fingernails; severe dizziness or fainting; confusion or unusual behavior; chest pain; seizures; severe constipation or stomach pain; signs of allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if you feel your pain is not being controlled, if you feel you are becoming dependent on the medicine, or if you experience mood changes, suicidal thoughts, or signs of adrenal problems such as unusual tiredness or weakness.
when_it_works: Immediate-release morphine usually begins to relieve pain within 30 minutes and the effect lasts about 4 to 6 hours. Extended-release morphine takes longer to start working — sometimes several hours — but provides steady pain relief over 8 to 24 hours. You should begin to notice improved pain control within the first day or two of starting treatment. If your pain is not adequately controlled after a few days, contact your doctor rather than taking extra doses on your own.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): You may be more sensitive to morphine's effects, especially dizziness, confusion, falls, and breathing problems. Your doctor will likely start you on a lower dose and monitor you closely. Pregnancy: Morphine can cause serious harm to an unborn baby, including neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome (NOWS) in newborns. Talk to your doctor right away if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Morphine passes into breast milk and can cause serious harm to a nursing baby. Do not breastfeed while taking morphine unless your doctor specifically advises it. Children: Morphine use in children must be carefully supervised by a doctor. Some forms of morphine are not approved for use in children. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver disease, as morphine can build up in your body and increase the risk of side effects.
